propositions.text: Principal Appellant, spouse, and children are Nigerian citizens appealing RPD decision denying refugee status.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Principal Appellant"), his spouse XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Associate Appellant") and their children, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Minor Appellants") are citizens of Nigeria.

propositions.text: RPD found appellants neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: They appeal the decision of the Refugee Protection Division ("RPD") dated March 10, 2020, whereby the RPD found that they were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection pursuant to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 ("IRPA").

propositions.text: Appellants ask RAD to set aside RPD decision and find them Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division ("RAD") to set aside the RPD decision and to find that they are Convention refuges and/or persons in need of protection pursuant to the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants are Nigerian citizens appealing the RPD decision denying refugee status and seeking RAD to set aside that decision.

propositions.text: Appellants tendered no new evidence under subsection 110(4) IRPA but requested oral hearing under subsection 110(6).
propositions.quote: The Appellants have tendered no new evidence under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, but have requested an oral hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes appellants submitted no new evidence but requested an oral hearing under IRPA provisions.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant appointed designated representative for Minor Appellants.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant has been appointed designated representative for the Minor Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Principal Appellant is designated representative for the minor appellants.

propositions.text: Confirms RPD decision appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: I hereby confirm the RPD decision that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees under section 96 of the IRPA, nor are they persons in need of protection within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Appeal is dismissed accordingly.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, this appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision denying refugee status and dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant claims employment with Nigerian bank and assignment to Ado Ekiti branch.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant claims to be a XXXX employed by the XXXX XXXX XXXX in Nigeria where he had been assigned to a XXXX XXXX in Ado Ekiti.

propositions.text: In August 2018, Principal Appellant investigated a defaulted loan involving fraudulent scheme by five individuals.
propositions.quote: In August 2018, his supervisor assigned him a file regarding a loan which had gone into default. He claims that in the course of the investigation, he discovered that a group of five individuals, the agents of persecution, had participated in a fraudulent scheme by which a loan was advanced by the bank to them who then split the proceeds of the loan.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the Principal Appellant's employment and investigation of a fraudulent loan scheme involving five individuals.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant alleges agents of persecution include banker, politician, politically connected individuals, and government official president of Cooperative Society.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant alleges that one of the agents of persecution is a banker, another is a highly situated state politician, two others are politically connected individuals who have run unsuccessfully for office and the fifth is a government official who has been described as the president of the Ado Ekiti Primary Healthcare Staff Cooperative Multipurpose Society ("Cooperative Society") which is the agency to which the loan was granted.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Principal Appellant alleges the agents of persecution include various politically connected individuals and a government official.

propositions.text: After report submission, Principal Appellant received threats, home break-in, and family assault; also alleged attempted kidnap and shooting.
propositions.quote: He claims that his home was broken into by three individuals who tied he and his family up, slapped him and stole their cellphones. The Appellants have also reported allegations of attempted kidnap and being shot at as part of their claim.

propositions.text: Persecutory conduct caused appellants to move twice within Nigeria but agents tracked them; they traveled to USA then Canada to claim refugee protection.
propositions.quote: This persecutory conduct caused the Appellants to move within Nigeria twice, but they claim that the agents of persecution were able to track them down. They obtained a travel visa to the United States of America ("USA") and departed Nigeria on XXXX XXXX, 2018, where they remained until XXXX XXXX, 2018, at which time they made their way to Canada, where they commenced a claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts threats, assaults, and flight within Nigeria, then travel to USA and Canada to claim refugee protection.

propositions.text: RAD reviews RPD decision on correctness standard with independent evidence examination.
propositions.quote: My role is to review the RPD decision on a standard of correctness after having conducted an independent examination of the evidence.

propositions.text: Exception: defer to RPD if it had meaningful advantage assessing oral or documentary evidence, which is not the case here.
propositions.quote: The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard or documentary evidence tendered at the hearing which may, in certain cases, allow me to defer to RPD findings. I do not believe the RPD enjoyed any such meaningful advantage in this matter and all evidence from the RPD hearing has been taken into consideration in arriving at my decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD reviews RPD decision on correctness standard and finds no reason to defer to RPD findings here.

propositions.text: RPD found credibility determinative and appellants failed to prove targeting by agents of persecution on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the determinative issue was credibility and that the Appellants had failed to meet their burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that they had been targeted by the agents of persecution and that they were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility was key and appellants failed to prove persecution or refugee status on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD breached natural justice by failing to produce complete hearing record.
propositions.quote: the failure of the RPD to produce a complete record of the hearing constitutes a breach of natural justice by denying the Appellants the opportunity to properly prepare and argue their appeal

propositions.text: RPD erred by misapprehending evidence and failing to engage meaningfully in credibility findings.
propositions.quote: the RPD erred by failing to meaningfully engage with and misapprehending the evidence before it when making credibility findings

propositions.text: RPD erred by making a hidden plausibility finding.
propositions.quote: the RPD erred by making a hidden plausibility finding

propositions.text: An oral hearing should be held under the circumstances.
propositions.quote: under the circumstances, an oral hearing should be held

propositions.text: Court not persuaded by arguments on natural justice breach, misapprehension, or oral hearing request.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by counsel's argument with respect to items (i), (ii) and (iv) above.

propositions.text: Court agrees RPD erred on hidden plausibility finding but it was not determinative or outcome-affecting.
propositions.quote: I agree that, with respect to item (iii), the RPD erred in making the impugned implausibility finding but, as set out below, I consider that such finding was not determinative of the issues, nor does it affect the outcome of my decision.

propositions.text: Request for oral hearing is denied.
propositions.quote: Request for an oral hearing is denied

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue four errors; court rejects three but agrees on one non-determinative error and denies oral hearing.

propositions.text: Oral hearing should be held to address outstanding credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that an oral hearing should be held in order to address any outstanding credibility concerns surrounding any of the Appellants' evidence.

propositions.text: They cite subsection 110(6) IRPA in support.
propositions.quote: In support of this proposition, they cite subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue for oral hearing to address credibility issues, citing IRPA subsection 110(6).

propositions.text: Subsections 110(3), (4), and (6) IRPA require new evidence for RAD to hold hearing on appeal.
propositions.quote: When read together, subsections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new evidence admitted in accordance with the provisions of subsection 110(4)

propositions.text: Hearing may be held if new evidence raises serious credibility issue central to RPD decision and could justify claim acceptance or rejection.
propositions.quote: in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD decision and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains RAD cannot hold hearing without new evidence raising serious credibility issues central to RPD decision.

propositions.text: Appellants submitted no new evidence; RAD must proceed without hearing and denies oral hearing request.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have submitted no new evidence in support of their appeal. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing in their appeal, and their application for an oral hearing is denied.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes no new evidence submitted; denies oral hearing and proceeds without hearing.

propositions.text: RPD failed to produce complete hearing record, breaching natural justice and denying procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD has failed to produce a complete record of the refugee proceeding which constitutes a breach of natural justice. They allege that portions of the hearing audio recording are completely inaudible and the recording as a whole is not comprehensible. As a result, they claim that the inadequate record has created a serious possibility that the Appellants have been denied procedural fairness in pursuing their appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue incomplete RPD hearing record breaches natural justice and denies procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Two transcript versions exist: unofficial by counsel and official IRB transcript from same audio recording.
propositions.quote: there are, in fact, two versions of the transcript at play. Counsel submitted one (unofficial) version with the Appellants' Record, whereas I have been provided with an official transcript prepared by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) from the same RPD audio recording of the proceeding as provided to counsel.

propositions.text: IRB transcript occasionally notes inaudible words but generally comprehensible and minor inconvenience only.
propositions.quote: I note that there is from time to time (as is frequently the case when dealing with transcripts) a notation that a comment or a word was uttered which is shown as "inaudible." ... Despite what I would describe as a minor inconvenience with respect to the occasional missing word, I found no difficulty in comprehending the evidence

propositions.text: Court able to follow testimony considering context and line of inquiry despite occasional inaudible words.
propositions.quote: I was able to follow along with the testimony by considering the line of inquiry and taking into context the question posed, as well as the response given.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds official IRB transcript mostly clear with minor inaudible words, enabling comprehension of testimony.

propositions.text: Appellants' cited transcript excerpts incomplete; IRB transcript provides complete, comprehensive responses.
propositions.quote: Though counsel's transcript features breaks in the Principal Appellant's response, the above response appearing in the IRB transcript is a complete and comprehensive response to the question put to the Principal Appellant by the RPD member.

propositions.text: Court listened to audio and confirmed IRB transcript accuracy for cited exchanges.
propositions.quote: In order to satisfy myself as to the accuracy of the IRB transcript, I have listened to the exchanges listed herein and have confirmed them to be accurately reported by the IRB transcript.

paragraphs.summary: Court confirms IRB transcript completeness and accuracy over appellants' incomplete transcript excerpts.

propositions.text: Further transcript excerpts incomplete in counsel's version but complete in IRB transcript.
propositions.quote: Immediately below this excerpt are further statements that appear incomplete in counsel's transcript yet, once again, the IRB transcript is complete.

propositions.text: IRB transcript provides full response to RPD member's question despite gaps in counsel's transcript.
propositions.quote: Again, the excerpt referenced by counsel represents another example where counsel's transcript is incomplete, yet the IRB transcript provides what appears to be a complete version of the Principal Appellant's response

paragraphs.summary: Court notes counsel's transcript gaps but IRB transcript provides full responses to questions.

propositions.text: Differences likely due to transcriptionist equipment, not audio recording quality, which is clear.
propositions.quote: I am led to believe that it is not a problem with the audio recording of the proceeding but, perhaps, an issue with the equipment used by the transcriptionist who prepared counsel's transcript.

propositions.text: IRB/RAD policy provides official transcript to counsel after RAD decision referencing it.
propositions.quote: It is also worthy of note that it is IRB/RAD policy to provide a copy of the IRB transcript to counsel following a RAD decision in which an official IRB transcript is referenced.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds transcript differences due to transcriptionist equipment, not audio quality, and notes policy to provide official transcript to counsel.

propositions.text: Court experienced only minor inconvenience from transcript issues and could fairly assess the matter.
propositions.quote: I find I have not suffered anything other than minor inconvenience in conducting my independent assessment of this matter.

propositions.text: No denial of natural justice from RPD hearing tape issues.
propositions.quote: I find that there has been no denial of natural justice occasioned by the RPD hearing tape.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds only minor inconvenience from transcript issues and no denial of natural justice.

propositions.text: RPD found credibility determinative and noted Principal Appellant's English proficiency and memory.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue for the RPD was credibility. Once again, in conducting my own independent assessment of this matter, I have reviewed the IRB transcript at length... The Principal Appellant testified in English and I noted that he was quite proficient in the language and that there were no instances where he... showed any signs of memory issues

propositions.text: Court independently reviewed transcripts and audio, finds IRB transcript more reliable with few inaudible words not hindering testimony comprehension.
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the IRB transcript at length, as well as portions of the transcript supplied by counsel and the RPD hearing audio recording, where necessary. I have noted that the IRB transcript is much more reliable than the Appellants' unofficial version as there are relatively few instances where an inaudible response was recorded.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant regularly asked for clarifications which RPD provided, indicating understanding of questions.
propositions.quote: the Principal Appellant quite regularly asked for clarification of questions which requests the RPD unfailingly obliged.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found credibility key; court independently finds IRB transcript reliable and Principal Appellant proficient and clear in testimony.

propositions.text: Credibility is the determinative issue for this appeal.
propositions.quote: Credibility remains the determinative issue for purpose of this appeal.

propositions.text: Credibility assessment starts with a presumption of truthfulness, rebuttable by contradictions or omissions.
propositions.quote: The starting point of any credibility assessment lies with the presumption of truthfulness;12 this presumption - sometimes referred to as the Maldonado presumption - holds that when a refugee claimant swears certain facts to be true, they are presumed truthful unless there be reason to doubt their veracity.

propositions.text: Credibility may be undermined by contradictions, inconsistencies, omissions, or missing expected documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The presumption is always rebuttable and may be displaced by an accumulation of contradictions, inconsistencies or omissions or where the documentary evidence fails to mention what one ordinarily might expect it to mention.

propositions.text: Both personal credibility and claim credibility must be assessed; if found wanting, claim success may be compromised.
propositions.quote: A refugee claimant's personal credibility and the credibility of the claim must be assessed by the decision-maker and, in both cases, if found wanting, may compromise the success of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court states credibility is key, starting with a presumption of truthfulness rebuttable by contradictions or omissions, affecting claim success.

propositions.text: The RPD misapprehended evidence from the National Documentation Package about Nigerian police reports.
propositions.quote: the Appellants specifically argue that: (i) the RPD misapprehended evidence that it had cited from the National Documentation Package ("NDP") regarding the Nigerian police reports;

propositions.text: The RPD erred in making an erroneous plausibility finding.
propositions.quote: and (ii) the RPD erred in making an erroneous plausibility finding.

propositions.text: The manner in which police reports were obtained is not credible and contradicts objective NDP evidence.
propositions.quote: Manner in which police reports were obtained is not credible and contradictory of objective NDP evidence

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the RPD misapprehended NDP evidence on police reports and erred in plausibility findings, challenging report credibility.

propositions.text: The police reports were unreliable and had no evidentiary weight due to differing process from NDP information.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the police reports were not reliable and could not be afforded any evidentiary weight for a number of reasons, one such reason being that the process by which the Appellants alleged they were obtained differed materially from information contained in the NDP.

propositions.text: The RPD failed to meaningfully engage with the NDP and misapprehended evidence; police reports were obtained by a relative after arrival in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Appellants allege that the RPD failed to meaningfully engage with the NDP and, as a result, grossly misapprehended the evidence and that the police reports were obtained by a relative in Nigeria at their behest after they had arrived in Canada.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant testified a relative went to the police station and obtained the reports without authorization letter or affidavit.
propositions.quote: Specifically, as testified by the Principal Appellant: "I asked him to go to the police station where we reported the case. And he went there and that was where they gave it to him."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found police reports unreliable due to process differences; appellants say reports were obtained by a relative without authorization.

propositions.text: RPD relied on NDP info that police reports can be obtained by authorized third parties, not in absentia, and affidavits require direct knowledge.
propositions.quote: the RPD relied upon information from the NDP which indicates that: (i) police reports can be obtained by a third party provided that the person to whom the documents were initially issued authorizes that third party to obtain a copy; 15 (ii) when specifically asked about obtaining a police report from abroad, a law associate indicated that a police report cannot be obtained "in absentia";16 and (iii) the "affidavit must be deposed by the person who has direct knowledge of the content of the affidavit and not a third party."17

propositions.text: The affidavit rule cited relates specifically to stolen goods or missing property allegations, which partly applies here.
propositions.quote: The comment referenced at item (iii) above was made specifically with respect to allegations of stolen goods or missing property. While the allegations made by the Appellants are much more encompassing than stolen property, there is that element to the claim since they allege that the men who broke into their house stole laptops and cellphones.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD relied on NDP that police reports require authorization, cannot be obtained in absentia, and affidavits need direct knowledge, relevant to stolen property claims.

propositions.text: The NDP's 'not in absentia' means affidavit must be from first-hand knowledge for initial complaint submission.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the portion of the NDP indicating that a police report cannot be obtained "in absentia" references the submission of a complaint to police for the first time which requires an affidavit to be deposed by someone with first hand knowledge of the matter reported.

propositions.text: The proper interpretation is that someone must attend police in person with affidavit or authorization to obtain reports abroad.
propositions.quote: By reading this Response to Information Request excerpt in a contextual manner, I am of the view that the proper interpretation is that when requesting a copy or copies of police reports from abroad, someone must attend the police station in person. If the person who attends the police station has no direct knowledge of the incident, he or she must present themselves armed with an affidavit (in the event the report deals with stolen goods or missing property) or some form of authorization from the party who does have direct knowledge of the incident.

propositions.text: Appellants' counsel presumes authorization was given to brother-in-law to collect reports.
propositions.quote: I note that on the issue of authorization, the Appellants indicate in their memorandum, "...the only thing he needed to do was authorize his brother-in-law to collect the copies on his behalf, which presumably he did"

propositions.text: No evidence supports that the Principal Appellant provided affidavit or authorization to brother-in-law; counsel's presumption is unpersuasive.
propositions.quote: With respect to counsel, the evidentiary record does not support the notion that the Principal Appellant provided his brother-in-law with an affidavit in prescribed form or a letter of authorization, and I do not accept counsel's presumption as compelling or persuasive.

propositions.text: Appellants had opportunity to submit such evidence after RPD decision but failed to do so.
propositions.quote: I note that the Appellants have had ample opportunity to submit such evidence, if it existed, since the RPD decision was rendered and to have it considered for admission as new evidence and have failed to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects appellants' interpretation of NDP and counsel's presumption of authorization, noting no evidence was submitted despite opportunity.

propositions.text: Accepting counsel's argument would mean no police report could be obtained in absentia as incident would be unreported.
propositions.quote: Moreover, to accept counsel's argument that it is only applicable where a report is being made in the first instance means that there would be no police report to obtain, in absentia or otherwise, because the incident would not have been reported as yet.

propositions.text: The RPD finding that the Principal Appellant's testimony conflicts with objective NDP evidence is confirmed.
propositions.quote: As such, I agree with and confirm the RPD finding that the Principal Appellant's testimony regarding the manner by which the police reports were obtained conflicts with the objective NDP evidence.

propositions.text: This conflict undermines the Appellants' credibility and the credibility of the claim regarding significant persecutory conduct.
propositions.quote: This undermines the Appellants' credibility and, as the police reports allegedly involve the reporting of, one of the most significant incidents of alleged persecutory conduct, this finding also undermines the credibility of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms RPD's finding that police report testimony conflicts with NDP, undermining appellants' credibility and claim.

propositions.text: RPD made uncontested adverse credibility findings including failure to produce or request XXXX XXXX, no follow-up with police, and likely fabricated chat messages.
propositions.quote: The RPD made several adverse credibility findings which appear to be uncontested. Examples of such findings are as follows: (i) the Principal Appellant's failure to produce the XXXX XXXX or to have requested a copy of it from his former employer; (ii) the Principal Appellant's failure to conduct any sort of follow up with police or to make enquiries as to the status of the XXXX XXXX - in fact, he did not even "Google" the incident on the internet to determine its status; (iii) certain "chat" messages tendered on the day of the hearing purportedly to establish attempts to secure corroborative documents from Nigeria were found by the RPD to have likely been fabricated to buttress the Appellants' account and were, therefore, unreliable;

propositions.text: Affidavits contained information likely originating from appellants, not first-hand knowledge, thus unreliable and given no weight.
propositions.quote: (iv) various affidavits were filled with information that likely originated with the Appellants and were not relating to first-hand knowledge of the affiants, in such a way that they were not found to be reliable and were not given any weight;

propositions.text: The XXXX report was given no weight as it relied on the Principal Appellant's self-report, found not credible on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: (v) the XXXX report of XXXX XXXX, received no weight owing to the degree upon which it relied on the self-report of the Principal Appellant whose account of the allegations was, on a balance of probabilities, not credible.

propositions.text: These uncontested negative credibility findings significantly impact the claim across many allegations and cannot be ignored.
propositions.quote: The fact that these negative credibility findings are uncontested impact the claim significantly across a broad range of allegations ranging from the police investigation to attempts to obtain corroborative documents to the self-reported impact of the alleged persecutory conduct which cannot be disregarded or ignored as they have clearly impact upon the credibility of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD's uncontested adverse credibility findings significantly undermine the appellants' claim and cannot be ignored.

propositions.text: The IRB transcript reveals additional credibility-impacting testimony not in the RPD decision.
propositions.quote: I might add that the IRB transcript discloses other aspects of the Appellants' testimony not included in the RPD decision but which warrant mention in my determination, as they also impact upon the credibility of the Principal Appellant's testimony.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant testified an agent handled US visa applications and he did not review them before submission.
propositions.quote: When questioned by the RPD about the process by which the family obtained their USA visas, the Principal Appellant testified that it had been handled by an agent and that he had not reviewed the visa applications before they were submitted.

propositions.text: Previously, he testified the visa application showed him working at XXXX XXXX.
propositions.quote: Previously, he had testified that the visa application had showed him as working at XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: When asked how he knew the application was correct if he never reviewed it, he gave evasive, speculative answers.
propositions.quote: When asked how he knew the application form correctly identified his employer if he had never reviewed the application, the Principal Appellant provides the following evasive and non-responsive answer which speculates as to what he might have done: No, because before I applied for the visa I must have got a letter of introduction from the XXXX to do that. That's why I'm sure that he can't - I want to believe that he couldn't have put anything (inaudible) because U.S. Consulate, they will ask for a letter from my office which I must have submitted before the application was processed.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes additional IRB testimony showing evasive answers by the Principal Appellant about US visa applications, impacting credibility.

propositions.text: Neighbour's affidavit details an incident with armed men at appellants' residence, but Principal Appellant's testimony omits neighbour's presence.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the neighbour's affidavit provides enriched detail with respect to allegations regarding the incident where the Appellants allege that three armed men entered their residence, slapped the Principal Appellant and forced the other Appellants to lie facedown on the floor while they stole laptops and cellphones.

propositions.text: Neighbour was present giving home lessons during incident, but Principal Appellant did not mention this in testimony or Basis of Claim.
propositions.quote: While the neighbour's affidavit refers to himself as the Minor Appellants' "personal home lesson teacher" and indicates that he was at the residence giving them a home lesson, the Principal Appellant's testimony makes no reference of the neighbour's presence, specifically referencing that the armed men "asked us to lie down flat, my wife and my children." Neither the Appellants' Basis of Claim nor the Principal Appellants' testimony mentions the fact that the neighbour was present, an omission which I find to be material and impacts upon credibility.

propositions.text: The inconsistency between neighbour's and Principal Appellant's accounts creates further credibility concerns about the claim.
propositions.quote: I am of the view that it would be reasonable to expect, if credible, that the neighbour's account of the incident and the Principal Appellant's account of the same incident, particularly with respect to the fact that an eyewitness may have been present at the time, would have been in alignment. Instead the inconsistency creates further credibility concerns regarding the Appellants' supporting document, the Principal Appellant's testimony and the credibility of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds a material omission about a neighbour's presence during an incident, creating credibility concerns for the appellants' claim.

propositions.text: The court may make independent credibility findings from the evidentiary record without raising a new issue requiring notice.
propositions.quote: Although I cannot raise a new issue without putting the parties on notice, I am entitled to make independent findings of credibility where credibility was (as is the case herein) an issue before the RPD and where the finding derives from the evidentiary record.

propositions.text: Federal Court in Sary held RAD did not raise a new issue by referencing evidence supporting RPD's credibility findings.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Federal Court in Sary states as follows: The situation is quite different in this case. The RAD did not raise a "new issue" by pointing out the contradiction between Mr. XXXX visa application and his testimony on how he found his job in TroisRivières. It simply made reference to another piece of evidence in the tribunal's file which supported the RPD's findings on Mr. XXXX lack of credibility.

propositions.text: Credibility was central to RPD decision and appeal; no extrinsic evidence was considered without opportunity to review.
propositions.quote: The RPD's decision and Mr. XXXX submissions dealt extensively with this credibility issue and the arguments in its regard. This is not a situation where the decision maker considered extrinsic evidence without giving Mr. XXXX the opportunity to review it. On the contrary, Mr. XXXX credibility constituted the very basis of the RPD's decision and the appeal filed by Mr. XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains it can make independent credibility findings from the record without raising new issues, citing Federal Court precedent.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant gave questionable, unreliable testimony on US visa and significant persecutory event, leading to negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: In this regard, the Principal Appellant provided questionable and unreliable testimony with respect to both the Appellants' US visa application and what is perhaps the most significant persecutory event alleged; accordingly, I draw a negative inference with respect to his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court draws a negative credibility inference from the Principal Appellant's questionable testimony on visa and persecution events.

propositions.text: RPD found it implausible that only Principal Appellant was targeted in the bank fraud investigation.
propositions.quote: The RPD found it implausible that only the Principal Appellant was targeted as a result of the investigation into the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: Appellants argue implausibility findings should only be made in the clearest circumstances.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that implausibility findings should only be made in the clearest of circumstances.

propositions.text: The implausibility finding is not solidly grounded in the clearest circumstances and is not supported by evidence.
propositions.quote: Based upon my review of the evidence and in light of the jurisprudence, I agree that it is an implausibility finding one which I am not at all certain is solidly grounded in the "clearest of circumstances." In this regard, I agree with the Appellants that the implausibility finding is not supported by the evidence,

propositions.text: Despite error in implausibility finding, multiple credibility issues mean it does not impact ultimate decision.
propositions.quote: however, in light of the multiple credibility issues discussed above, it does not impact upon my ultimate decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the RPD's implausibility finding lacks clear support but finds it does not affect the ultimate decision due to other credibility issues.

propositions.text: Despite implausibility error, appellants failed to credibly establish bank fraud and persecution claims on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: Regardless of my finding that the RPD erred in the implausibility finding regarding the Principal Appellant (and his family) being the sole targets of the agents of persecution, as a result of a number of credibility issues - both uncontested and contested - the Appellants have failed to credibly establish, on a balance of probabilities, the allegations of bank fraud and the participation of the agents of persecution, not to mention the persecutory actions which they claim followed.

propositions.text: Appellants have not established a serious possibility of persecution or need for protection if returned to Nigeria; appeal fails.
propositions.quote: As a result, I find that on a forward-looking basis, the Appellants have not established that, if returned to Nigeria, they face a serious possibility of persecution based on a Convention ground, nor have they established, on a balance of probabilities, that they are persons in need of protection. As such, the appeal must necessarily fail.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes appellants failed to prove persecution or protection need; appeal is dismissed despite implausibility error.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed and the RPD decision confirmed that appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision denying refugee or protection status under IRPA.
